title: Split by the restriction that changes the choices
source: Count outcomes once, using complete cases

chunks.text: This section is called Split by the restriction that changes the choices. A useful case division has two properties: the cases cannot overlap, and together they cover every legal outcome. Choose a feature that controls the remaining choices. In a digit problem, the last digit or the position of zero may be more restrictive than the first digit. Fixing that feature can turn a confusing count into several straightforward products. SEE IT A complement needs a visible universe Each switch has two states, so the universe has four complete outcomes.

Only ON, ON is forbidden; subtracting it leaves three. Multiply within a case when successive choices build one complete outcome. Add across disjoint cases. Do not assume every case has the same number of choices. A leading-zero rule, a required neighbour or a fixed position can make one branch smaller than another. A095 and A101 are useful for reading such restrictions without replacing them by a more familiar but different question. Sometimes it is easier to count everything and subtract the forbidden outcomes.

This complement method needs a clear universe: what exactly is included in “everything”? If two forbidden conditions can occur together, subtracting their counts separately may remove an outcome twice. Either separate them into disjoint classes or restore the overlap. A048 is a place to compare direct counting with a carefully defined complement. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Prove that the classification is reversible
source: Count outcomes once, using complete cases

chunks.text: This section is called Prove that the classification is reversible. A strong counting method gives each outcome an address in your list of cases. From an outcome, you should be able to recover the choices that produced it. Conversely, every allowed choice in the method should build a valid outcome. This two-way check proves completeness and prevents double counting. It is often more convincing than a second long multiplication. Neighbour restrictions can sometimes be handled by placing separator objects first and using the gaps around them.

Restrictions on misplaced objects can be handled by describing how positions send objects around cycles. N2.26 and N1.27 develop these different representations. The representation must capture the actual rule; the same convenient picture should not be reused when a changed condition invalidates it. Be especially careful when several action histories can produce one final object. Classify the final structures, or identify precisely which histories merge together. N4.28 asks for this distinction. For an independent check, list the smallest meaningful cases or use a different classification.

A computer enumeration can confirm a count, but the written explanation should still make clear why every legal outcome has one place in the argument. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
source: Count outcomes once, using complete cases

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Count outcomes once, using complete cases. Let the restriction split the cases A lunch contains one sandwich, cheese or bean, and one fruit, apple, pear or plum. Cheese may not be paired with plum. How many different legal lunches are there? The branches have different sizes because the restriction affects only cheese. Multiply the numbers of choices within each case, then add the disjoint case totals. Work through the example 1. Split by sandwich.

These cases cannot overlap because a lunch contains exactly one sandwich. 2. With cheese, the permitted fruits are apple and pear: two lunches. 3. With bean, all three fruits are permitted: three lunches. 4. Add the disjoint cases: 2+3=5. Each leaf names its sandwich and fruit, so every legal lunch appears exactly once. As a check, 2 times 3-1=5 counts all pairs and removes cheese with plum. Answer. There are 5 different legal lunches. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook.

title: Count incidences before counting objects
source: Count the same structure from two directions

chunks.text: This section is called Count incidences before counting objects. An incidence is a meeting between an object and one of its features: a bridge and an endpoint, a shape and an edge, or a member and a group. You do not need to remember the word to use the idea. Ask what is being counted when each local object reports its own contribution, and how many reports refer to the same underlying thing. SEE IT Every edge reports at two ends The graph has five edges.

Its four vertices report degrees 3, 2, 3 and 2, totalling ten because each edge meets two vertices. In a network where every edge joins two vertices, adding all vertex degrees counts each edge twice. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it. Thus the degree total equals twice the edge count. The same reasoning explains why the degree total is even. An odd total is impossible, regardless of how many different drawings have been tried.

For a solid assembled from faces, adding the face-edge counts may count shared edges twice. For a row of joined objects, a new object may share part of the previous boundary. A074 and A096 reward tracking which pieces are genuinely new. The useful count is determined by the joining rule, not by multiplying the size of one separate object by the number of objects. title: Give each component its contribution
source: Count the same structure from two directions

chunks.text: This section is called Give each component its contribution. Suppose several measurements each include some of the same unknown quantities. Adding the measurements can be useful if every unknown appears equally often. Then the sum is a fixed multiple of the desired total. If one unknown appears more often, the extra contribution must be kept rather than silently discarded. A076 and A132 develop these related forms of bookkeeping.

SEE IT A table reveals the repeated copies A 1 records one appearance of that component in the column’s pair total; a 0 records none. Each row totals two, so adding the three measurements doubles a+b+c. A contribution table can organise the argument without introducing many equations. Put one underlying component in each row and record how often it appears in each measurement. The row total tells you its coefficient in the combined sum. This explains why a particular addition or subtraction isolates the requested quantity.

It also helps you notice when a visually central component is counted more often than an outer one. The same method works with two overlapping sets. An object in one set contributes once to the sum of set sizes; an object in two sets contributes twice. Subtracting the overlap once counts each object in the union once. If you want objects belonging to exactly one set, the double-counted overlap must be removed twice. Always name the desired region before choosing the correction. title: Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound
source: Count the same structure from two directions

chunks.text: This section is called Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound. If every proposed group uses a fixed number of pairs, and no pair may be reused, the available pairs place an upper bound on the number of groups. The argument does not require constructing the groups first. Count the resource each group consumes and compare it with the total resource available. N2.30 uses this kind of incidence budget. A bound is only half an optimization solution.

It proves that exceeding a number is impossible, but does not prove that the number can be reached. After obtaining the bound, construct an arrangement and check every rule. In a group-design problem, verify that no pair is repeated; in a scheduling problem, verify that no participant has conflicting assignments. A list that looks orderly can still conceal a repeated pair. Local counting can also reveal hidden global information.

Different kinds of events may distribute different total contributions, so a known grand total determines how many events of each kind occurred. N2.27 combines this observation with a further restriction on a selected group. A139 similarly rewards noticing unequal incidences before trying placements. The general habit is to count contributions first and use the resulting structure to guide the construction. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Count the same structure from two directions
source: Count the same structure from two directions

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Count the same structure from two directions. Remove the two reports at each join Four unit squares form a 2-by-2 square. Find the outside perimeter by first counting the edges of the separate tiles. Coral dashed edges lie inside the completed square. Each was counted twice in the original tile reports, and neither report belongs to the outside boundary. Work through the example 1. Four separate tiles report 4 times 4=16 unit edges. 2.

After joining, there are four internal shared unit edges: two along the vertical middle line and two along the horizontal middle line. 3. Each internal edge was reported by both tiles beside it. Remove two reports at each of the four joins: 16-2 times 4=8. 4. The outside outline is a square with side 2, so its perimeter is also 4 times 2=8 units. This checks the contribution count. Answer. The outside perimeter is 8 units. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook.

title: Find a resource that every arrangement uses
source: Prove a limit, then build an example

chunks.text: This section is called Find a resource that every arrangement uses. For a maximum, look for something limited: available positions, pairs, edges, total weight or total sum. Show how much of that resource each selected object must use. This gives an upper bound. For a minimum, ask what every arrangement must contain or cover. The same limited resource may force at least a certain number of objects, steps or days.

SEE IT A bound and the arrangement that reaches it Group positions into the four adjacent pairs (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) and (7,8). Each pair holds at most one counter. The shown four-counter arrangement also obeys the neighbour rule across pairs. For a connected shape whose boundary follows horizontal and vertical grid lines, use the smallest enclosing grid rectangle, of width w and height h. The area is at most wh.

The boundary contains at least 2w of horizontal segments and at least 2h of vertical segments, so its perimeter is at least 2(w+h). This perimeter argument depends on the grid-aligned edges; it does not apply unchanged to curved or diagonal boundaries. A028 is useful for distinguishing this bound from an actual arrangement that meets the tiling rules. Use all restrictions that can tighten the bound. A rough count may allow an extreme value that parity or distinctness later forbids.

N1.30 develops this idea: a first counting bound is only a starting point, and a second kind of information can exclude equality. Do not discard a rough bound because it is not sharp immediately. It may reduce the problem to one critical case. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. title: Explain why a promising choice is best
source: Prove a limit, then build an example

chunks.text: This section is called Explain why a promising choice is best. When a fixed total is split into positive parts, balanced parts often give a larger product. For two parts with sum S, the product can be written S squared/4-(x-S/2) squared. The squared term is nonnegative, so moving x closer to the midpoint increases the product. This explains the tendency; it is not just a pattern seen in a few calculations.

SEE IT Balancing the sides increases the product These are all positive integer side-length pairs with sum 6, up to exchanging the sides. Each rectangle has perimeter 12, while its area rises from 5 to 8 to 9 as the sides become closer. Restrictions may prevent perfect balance. The parts may need to be whole numbers, distinct, or drawn from a specified set. Then find the most balanced permitted choices and prove that no other legal choice gives a better value.

With more parts, an exchange argument can help: if transferring a little from an overly large part to a smaller one improves the product while preserving legality, the original arrangement was not optimal. Place-value problems use a different comparison. A digit moved to a more valuable position can outweigh all later changes, but leading-zero restrictions must be preserved. An exchange proof must describe a legal swap, not an ideal rearrangement that leaves the allowed set.

A084 and A134 are useful for checking the boundary cases where a seemingly obvious greedy choice needs more careful justification. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Make equality conditions guide the construction
source: Prove a limit, then build an example

chunks.text: This section is called Make equality conditions guide the construction. After deriving a bound, inspect the places where equality would be needed. If the proof says that each day can hold at most a certain number of disjoint activities, a minimum schedule must use that capacity efficiently. If a local restriction forbids connections within a group, try placing the remaining connections between groups. N1.29 illustrates how the proof can suggest the attaining arrangement. Check the construction independently. Verify every original requirement, not just the numerical total.

A candidate might reach the bound while repeating a forbidden pair, overlapping pieces, using a value twice or violating a strict inequality. Record the checks in an organised way so that the reader can see why the witness is legal. An attractive picture or a long list does not certify itself. Sometimes the correct conclusion is that the first bound cannot be attained. Then explain the obstruction and seek the next possible value.

For a largest impossible total, reverse the usual task: prove one value impossible and construct every larger value. N3.29 uses a finite set of starting constructions together with a repeatable extension. That final extension is what turns a finite check into a statement about an unlimited range. title: Prove a limit, then build an example
source: Prove a limit, then build an example

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Prove a limit, then build an example. Use the tighter capacity bound Pack 7 red counters and 4 blue counters into trays. A tray holds at most 4 counters in total, and at most 2 of them may be red. What is the smallest possible number of trays? Empty circles are unused capacity. Leaving some spaces empty is necessary because red capacity, rather than total capacity, gives the decisive bound. Work through the example 1. There are 11 counters altogether.

Since one tray holds at most 4, at least 3 trays are needed. This is only a first bound. 2. The red counters give a stronger bound: three trays can hold at most 3 times 2=6 red counters. There are 7 red counters, so at least 4 trays are necessary. 3. Use the four trays shown: RRBB, RRB, RRB and R. They contain 7 red and 4 blue counters. 4. The tray sizes are 4, 3, 3 and 1, all at most 4.

Their red counts are 2, 2, 2 and 1, all at most 2. The construction meets every rule and reaches the lower bound. Answer. Exactly 4 trays are needed. title: Build an honest sample space
source: Let the experiment determine the probability

chunks.text: This section is called Build an honest sample space. A sample space is the collection of possible complete outcomes. For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of all outcomes. Equal likelihood is an assumption to justify from the experiment. Two colour names are not automatically equally likely just because there are two names. SEE IT Colours can collect different numbers of outcomes R₁, R₂ and B₁ label three physical counters.

Each has probability 1/3, but red collects two of those equal possibilities. Labelling individual objects can reveal the true outcomes. If a bag contains a red counters and b blue counters, a uniform choice gives each individual counter probability 1/(a+b). The colour red then collects a of those equal possibilities, giving probability a/(a+b). Different colours may collect different numbers of individual outcomes. The labels help the reasoning even when they are not printed on the actual counters. Choosing a bag first can change the weights.

If bags have different sizes, an equally likely bag choice does not make every counter equally likely. A counter in a smaller chosen bag receives a larger share of that bag's probability. Keep both stages in the description. Pooling the objects is a different experiment unless the bag probabilities have been chosen to give every individual object the same overall chance. title: Track how one choice changes the next
source: Let the experiment determine the probability

chunks.text: This section is called Track how one choice changes the next. For successive choices, an ordered outcome records what happened first and what happened next. Along one route, multiply the probability of the first event by the probability of the second event given that first event. Add routes only when they are disjoint: a single completed experiment cannot follow two different complete routes at once. This is the reasoning behind a probability tree.

SEE IT Update the bag before following the next branch At each draw, every remaining counter is equally likely. After red is drawn, one red and one blue remain. After blue is drawn, both remaining counters are red. Multiply along each complete route; the route probabilities sum to 1. Without replacement, the available collection changes. After a specified colour is removed, both its count and the total count may change. Write the updated composition before calculating the second probability.

With replacement and a fresh uniform selection, the original composition is restored. The second choice then has the same colour probabilities regardless of the first. The wording of the selection process decides which model applies. An unordered pair can also be a useful outcome when the final event ignores order. But the numerator and denominator must use the same kind of object. Counting favourable unordered pairs and dividing by all ordered draws mixes two sample spaces.

A check is to convert the entire calculation to the other model and confirm that the fraction agrees, explaining how many orders correspond to each unordered pair. title: Recount within the information you are given
source: Let the experiment determine the probability

chunks.text: This section is called Recount within the information you are given. A conditional probability asks for a chance after some information is known. Imagine crossing out every outcome inconsistent with that information. The remaining outcomes form the new comparison group. If the original outcomes were equally likely, the conditional probability is the favourable surviving count divided by the total surviving count. The denominator is no longer the size of the original sample space. If outcomes have unequal weights, crossing out is still a useful picture, but counts alone are insufficient.

Add the probabilities of the surviving outcomes and compare the favourable surviving probability with that total. In symbols, P(E given F)=P(E and F)/P(F), provided P(F)>0. The denominator rescales the surviving group so that its total probability becomes one. This explains the formula rather than presenting it as a rule to memorise. N2.28 is a place to distinguish an object's colour from its physical identity and to keep a full record of the choices. Labelled histories can make the condition precise.

After solving, check whether every favourable history satisfies the stated information. Also check the final request: a contest may ask for a quantity formed from a simplified fraction, rather than for the fraction itself. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Let the experiment determine the probability
source: Let the experiment determine the probability

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Let the experiment determine the probability. Shrink the comparison group Two fair coins are flipped independently. You are told that at least one of the coins is heads. What is the probability that both are heads? Crossing out TT changes the comparison group from four outcomes to three. HT and TH stay separate because the coins have distinct positions. Work through the example 1. Record the first coin and second coin separately.

The four complete outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT each have probability 1/4. 2. The information “at least one is heads” removes TT and keeps HH, HT and TH. 3. The three surviving outcomes are still equally likely. Only HH has both coins heads. 4. Use the surviving group as the denominator: 1 favourable outcome out of 3 surviving outcomes gives probability 1/3. Answer. The conditional probability is 1/3. title: Keep the whole visible
source: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree

chunks.text: This section is called Keep the whole visible. A fraction describes a number of equal parts relative to a chosen whole. Before using it, name that whole. A fraction of an original amount and the same fraction of a remainder usually describe different quantities. Successive changes should be recorded as multipliers acting on the current amount. An increase and a decrease by matching percentage labels therefore need not cancel.

SEE IT An overlap shows a fraction of a fraction Select three of the four columns, then take two of the three rows of that selection. The purple overlap contains six of the rectangle’s twelve equal cells. To add fractions, express them using equal-sized parts. A common denominator provides that shared unit; it does not change the quantities being added. To multiply fractions, multiply the corresponding scale factors. To divide by a nonzero fraction, ask what starting quantity would produce the known result when multiplied by that fraction.

This connection with inverse operations gives meaning to multiplying by the reciprocal. A fraction of a fraction is a product of scale factors, while a difference of fractions of the same whole can reveal the whole. In A017, identify which changes refer to one fixed capacity before setting up the calculation. In A094, equal fractional parts create a relationship between two different group sizes. The fractions may be equal amounts without being equal fractions of the same-sized whole. Before moving on, open your notebook.

title: Read decimal places as divisibility conditions
source: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree

chunks.text: This section is called Read decimal places as divisibility conditions. A terminating decimal with at most k places is an integer divided by 10k. Therefore multiplying it by 10k gives an integer. This is a useful test because it turns a statement about written digits into a divisibility condition. Leading zeros after the decimal point still occupy places; trailing zeros can be removed without changing the value. SEE IT Build a power of ten from prime partners Forty supplies three 2s but only one 5.

Two additional 5s pair with the unpaired 2s, making three factors of 10. Multiply the numerator by the same 25 to preserve the fraction. In lowest terms, a fraction terminates exactly when its denominator contains no primes except two and five. Every power of ten is built from those primes. If the reduced denominator has only those factors, multiplying by enough missing copies turns it into a power of ten. If another prime remains, no power of ten can supply it. Cancellation must happen before applying this test.

For a positive integer k, exactly k decimal places means at most k places but not at most k-1 places after unnecessary trailing zeros are removed. N4.27 develops this distinction. It is often cleaner to count the broader divisibility condition and subtract the smaller one. For decimal shifts, track the place-value multiplier instead of moving a written point without explanation. A119 rewards interpreting the change as an exact fraction of the shifted quantity. title: Transform equations without losing conditions
source: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree

chunks.text: This section is called Transform equations without losing conditions. An equation states that two expressions have the same value. Adding the same quantity to both sides preserves that equality. Multiplying both sides by the same nonzero quantity also preserves it and can clear denominators. Before dividing by an expression containing a variable, check that it cannot be zero; otherwise you may remove a possible case or use an invalid step. Choose transformations that reveal structure. A product condition invites factorisation, while several weighted sums may invite addition or subtraction.

Expanding (x-a)(y-b) gives xy-bx-ay+ab. Reading that identity backwards shows how a combination of a product and two linear terms might become a factor-pair problem after adding the right constant. N2.29 is a place to connect an algebraic transformation with a finite, organised count. Keep the domain visible throughout: positive integers, digits, lengths or unrestricted numbers are different allowed sets. Algebra may produce a value that violates one of those meanings. A062 and A088 require bounds on digits as well as equations.

After finding candidates, substitute them into the original relationship and check every domain restriction. Reversible algebra explains why none were lost; the final checks explain why the survivors are valid. Before moving on, open your notebook.
